claim: Mature T cells bearing αβ T cell receptors react with foreign antigens bound to alleles of major histocompatibility complex proteins (MHC) that they were exposed to during their development in the thymus.
source: Mature T cells bearing αβ T cell receptors react with foreign antigens bound to alleles of major histocompatibility complex proteins (MHC) that they were exposed to during their development in the thymus, a phenomenon known as positive selection.
evidence: This is a well-established phenomenon in immunology supported by extensive prior research and is stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Positive selection-induced MHC bias of T cell receptors is affected by the germline encoded elements of the T cell receptor α and β chain.
source: Here, using mice expressing one of two different T cell receptor β chains and various MHC alleles, we show that positive selection-induced MHC bias of T cell receptors is affected both by the germline encoded elements of the T cell receptor α and β chain
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mice expressing different TCR β chains and MHC alleles, as described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Positive selection-induced MHC bias of T cell receptors is dramatically affected by the non germ line encoded portions of CDR3 of the T cell receptor α chain.
source: Here, using mice expressing one of two different T cell receptor β chains and various MHC alleles, we show that positive selection-induced MHC bias of T cell receptors is affected both by the germline encoded elements of the T cell receptor α and β chain and, surprisingly, dramatically affected by the non germ line encoded portions of CDR3 of the T cell receptor α chain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by sequencing data and statistical analyses comparing CDR3α sequences across different MHC alleles.

claim: The non germline encoded elements of T cell receptors may help the proteins cope with the extremely polymorphic nature of major histocompatibility complex products within the species.
source: Thus, in addition to determining specificity for antigen, the non germline encoded elements of T cell receptors may help the proteins cope with the extremely polymorphic nature of major histocompatibility complex products within the species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings regarding the role of non-germline encoded TCR elements.

claim: T cell antigen receptors are composed of alpha and beta chains (TCRs) that react with peptides derived from pathogens bound in a groove on the surface of host major histocompatibility proteins (MHCs).
source: Many T lymphocytes in the body express clonally distributed T cell antigen receptors composed of alpha and beta chains (TCRs) that react with peptides derived from pathogens and other foreign materials bound in a groove on the surface of host major histocompatibility proteins (MHCs) (Allison et al., 1982; Babbitt et al., 1985; Haskins et al., 1983; Meuer et al., 1983; Shimonkevitz et al., 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology supported by multiple citations.

claim: The genes encoding MHC proteins are the most polymorphic genes in a given species.
source: The genes encoding these MHC proteins are the most polymorphic genes in a given species.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology and genetics.

claim: Most of the polymorphisms in MHC proteins tend to be concentrated within the residues that line the peptide-binding groove of the molecules.
source: Most of the polymorphisms tend to be concentrated within the residues that line the peptide-binding groove of the molecules (Bjorkman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Different MHC alleles within a species preferentially bind and present different peptides from any given invading organism.
source: Hence, in general, different MHC alleles within a species preferentially bind, and present to TCRs, different peptides from any given invading organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the polymorphic nature of MHC molecules and established immunological knowledge.

claim: The allelic variants of MHC expressed in one individual are very frequently recognized by 1% or more of the T cells of other individuals expressing different MHC alleles.
source: The allelic variants of MHC expressed in one individual are very frequently recognized by 1% or more of the T cells of other individuals expressing different MHC alleles, a phenomenon called 'alloreactivity'.
evidence: This is established knowledge about alloreactivity in immunology.

claim: Differences in bound peptides play an important role in alloreactivity.
source: While differences in bound peptides play an important role in alloreactivity (Hunt et al., 1990; Crumpacker et al., 1992), structural studies show that some of the allelic variations in MHC proteins themselves interact with the TCRs of alloreactive T cells (Grandea and Bevan, 1993; Archbold et al., 2008; Colf et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some of the allelic variations in MHC proteins themselves interact with the TCRs of alloreactive T cells.
source: While differences in bound peptides play an important role in alloreactivity (Hunt et al., 1990; Crumpacker et al., 1992), structural studies show that some of the allelic variations in MHC proteins themselves interact with the TCRs of alloreactive T cells (Grandea and Bevan, 1993; Archbold et al., 2008; Colf et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: T cells in one individual are more likely to react with foreign peptides bound to the grooves of self MHC than to foreign peptides bound to foreign MHC.
source: Experiments have shown that T cells in one individual are more likely to react with foreign peptides bound to the grooves of self MHC than to foreign peptides bound to foreign MHC (Fink and Bevan, 1978; Zinkernagel et al., 1978; Kappler and Marrack, 1978; Sprent, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to classic experiments demonstrating MHC restriction.

claim: Thymocytes are allowed to develop into mature T cells only if the TCR they bear reacts with low affinity/avidity with MHC proteins bound to self peptides in the thymus.
source: This phenomenon, known to be the consequence of thymic positive selection, is caused by the fact that thymocytes are allowed to develop into mature T cells only if the TCR they bear reacts with low affinity/avidity with MHC proteins bound to self peptides in the thymus (Sprent et al., 1988; Ashton-Rickardt et al., 1994; Sebzda et al., 1994; Hogquist et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about positive selection supported by multiple citations.

claim: The thymus generally weeds out T cell progenitors that react with too high affinity/avidity with self MHC plus self peptide through negative selection.
source: Paradoxically, in an apoptotic process termed 'negative selection', the thymus generally weeds out T cell progenitors that react with too high affinity/avidity with self MHC plus self peptide, thus preventing the maturation of many potentially self reactive T cells (Kappler et al., 1987; von Boehmer et al., 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about negative selection supported by citations.

claim: The alpha and beta chains that comprise TCRs each usually engage MHC + peptide via three complementary determining loops (CDRs 1,2 and 3).
source: Mutational and structural studies have shown that the alpha and beta chains that comprise TCRs each usually engage MHC + peptide via three complementary determining loops (CDRs 1,2 and 3) (Garcia et al., 1996; Reinherz et al., 1999; Dai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by mutational and structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: For both the TCR alpha and beta chains, CDR1 and CDR2 loops are encoded by the germ line Trav and Trbv genes.
source: For both the TCR alpha and beta chains, two of these loops, CDR1 and CDR2, are encoded by the germ line Trav (for the TCRα chain) and Trbv (for the TCRβ chain) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR gene structure.

claim: The CDR3 loop for each TCR chain is produced during TCR gene rearrangement as the cells develop in the thymus.
source: The third, CDR3, loop for each chain, on the other hand, is produced during TCR gene rearrangement as the cells develop in the thymus (Davis, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR gene rearrangement supported by citation.

claim: The sequence coding for CDR3α is created when one of many Trav gene segments rearranges to fuse with one of the many Traj gene segments with the total number of possible CDR3α sequences increased by removal and/or addition of bases at the joining points.
source: Thus, the sequence coding for CDR3α, for example, is created when one of many Trav gene segments rearranges to fuse with one of the many Traj gene segments with the total number of possible CDR3α sequences increased by removal and/or addition of bases at the joining points of Trav and Traj (Gellert, 2002; Cabaniols et al., 2001; Moshous et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about V(D)J recombination supported by citations.

claim: TCR CDR3 loops contact peptide.
source: Indeed evidence that the CDR3 loops contact peptide rapidly appeared (Danska et al., 1990; Kelly et al., 1993; Wither et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TCRs are usually oriented diagonally on the MHC, but the angle of their interaction varies quite considerably from one structure to another.
source: However, when crystallographically solved structures of TCRs on MHC became available it was soon apparent that TCRs are usually oriented diagonally on the MHC, but the angle of their interaction varies quite considerably from one structure to another.
evidence: This is based on structural studies of TCR-MHC complexes.

claim: The TCR CDR3 regions are often focused on the peptide, but amino acids in these regions sometimes also contact MHC.
source: Although the TCR CDR3 regions are often focused on the peptide, amino acids in these regions sometimes also contact MHC and, vice versa, CDR1 and CDR2 amino acids sometimes contact peptide in addition to their predicted interactions with MHC(Garboczi et al., 1996; Garcia et al., 1996; Hennecke and Wiley, 2001; Meuer et al., 1983; Rudolph et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: CDR1 and CDR2 amino acids sometimes contact peptide in addition to their predicted interactions with MHC.
source: Although the TCR CDR3 regions are often focused on the peptide, amino acids in these regions sometimes also contact MHC and, vice versa, CDR1 and CDR2 amino acids sometimes contact peptide in addition to their predicted interactions with MHC(Garboczi et al., 1996; Garcia et al., 1996; Hennecke and Wiley, 2001; Meuer et al., 1983; Rudolph et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The entire sequence of the TCRα chain, including the TRAV, TRAJ and CDR3α, is involved in positive selection.
source: Understanding of this issue is complicated by the cooperative nature of TCR interactions with its ligands, by which an interaction at one site on the TCR/MHC/peptide surface adjusts interactions elsewhere (Mazza et al., 2007; Baker et al., 2012; Adams et al., 2016) and a study that indicated that the entire sequence of the TCRα chain, including the TRAV, TRAJ and CDR3α, is involved in positive selection (Merkenschlager et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A fairly high percentage of individual TCRα or TCRβ sequences are expressed in animals regardless of their MHC haplotype.
source: This is because others and we have found a fairly high percentage of individual TCRα or TCRβ sequences are expressed in animals regardless of their MHC haplotype (Robins et al., 2010; Warren et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2014) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data in the supplementary file.

claim: Each individual TCR chain is paired with a different partner(s) in animals with different MHC alleles.
source: Presumably this is at least in part possible because each individual chain is paired with a different partner(s) in animals with different MHC alleles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that individual chains appear across different MHC haplotypes.

claim: The T cells in any given mouse or human have been reported to bear, collectively, more than 10^5 different TCRα and about the same number of different TCRβ chain sequences.
source: The T cells in any given mouse or human have been reported to bear, collectively, more than 105 different TCRαand about the same number of different TCRβ chain sequences (Venturi et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The T cells might bear up to 10^10 different combinations of TCR alpha and beta chains.
source: Thus the T cells might bear up to 1010 different combinations of these chains.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the number of different alpha and beta chains.

claim: Only a limited number of TCRα chains can be positively selected with a single TCRβ.
source: This choice has two advantages. It allowed accurate knowledge of the TCRβ on the T cells and, because it was expected that only a limited number of TCRα chains can be positively selected with a single TCRβ, it limited the numbers of different TCRαsequences we expected to find in the mice (Merkenschlager et al., 1994; Fukui et al., 1998; Hsieh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The DOβ48A mutation reduces the ability of the TCRβ chain to react with the alpha chain alpha helix of MHCII and with the alpha1 alpha helix of MHCI.
source: This mutation reduces the ability of the TCRβ chain to react with the alpha chain alpha helix of MHCII and with the alpha1 alpha helix of MHCI.
evidence: This is based on previous characterization of the DOβ48A mutation.

claim: The numbers of mature CD4 or CD8 thymocytes in mice expressing DOβ48A were much lower than those in mice expressing DOβWT.
source: As predicted by our previous data using retrogenic mice (Scott-Browne et al., 2009), the numbers of mature CD4 or CD8 thymocytes in mice expressing DOβ48A were much lower than those in mice expressing DOβWT (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The TCRβ 48A for 48Y substitution affects MHC interactions regardless of the MHC class or allele.
source: Thus the TCRβ 48A for 48Y substitution affects MHC interactions regardless of the MHC class or allele, as we have previously predicted (Scott-Browne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing reduced thymocyte numbers across different MHC alleles, supported by previous predictions.

claim: The difference in numbers of mature T cells between mice expressing DOβWT and DOβ48A was less marked in peripheral lymph nodes than in the thymus.
source: The difference in numbers of mature T cells between mice expressing DOβWT and DOβ48A was less marked in peripheral lymph nodes than in the thymus (Figure 1B), probably because of increased homeostatic expansion, as exemplified by the increased percentages of CD44hi T cells amongst those few that could mature in DOβ48A mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: There were more mature CD4 than CD8 T cells in the lymph nodes of mice expressing DOβWT and H2b.
source: There were more mature CD4 than CD8 T cells in the lymph nodes of mice expressing DOβWT and H2b (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The bias towards CD4 versus CD8 T cells in H2b animals may be due to the fact that DOβWT was found in a TCR that reacts with IAd or IAb plus a foreign peptide and not from an MHCI-reactive TCR.
source: The phenomenon may be due to the fact that DOβWT was found in a TCR that reacts with IAd or IAb plus a foreign peptide (OVA 327–339) and not from an MHCI-reactive TCR (White et al., 1983).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed CD4/CD8 bias, supported by citation to the origin of DOβWT.

claim: DOβWT transduced cells from a DOβ48A H2b mouse were most likely to react with H2b presenting cells.
source: For example, T cells from a DOβ48A H2b mouse, after transduction to express DOβWT, were most likely to react with H2b presenting cells and DOβWT transduced cells from DOβ48A H2s mice reacted only with challenge cells expressing H2s.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the retroviral transduction experiments.

claim: DOβWT transduced cells from DOβ48A H2s mice reacted only with challenge cells expressing H2s.
source: For example, T cells from a DOβ48A H2b mouse, after transduction to express DOβWT, were most likely to react with H2b presenting cells and DOβWT transduced cells from DOβ48A H2s mice reacted only with challenge cells expressing H2s.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the retroviral transduction experiments.

claim: The TCRα chain that pairs with the transgenic DOβ48A contributes to the preference of CD4 T cells to react with peptides bound to the MHCII allele involved in positive selection.
source: These experiments show that the TCRα chain that pairs with the transgenic DOβ48A does indeed contribute to the preference of CD4 T cells to react with peptides bound to the MHCII allele involved in positive selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the retroviral transduction experiments showing MHC-specific reactivity.

claim: The T cells in mice expressing a single TCRβ chain have a limited repertoire of TCRα chains by comparison with WT animals.
source: Others have previously reported that the T cells in mice expressing a single TCRβ chain have a limited repertoire of TCRα chains by comparison with WT animals (Fukui et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The total number of TCRα sequences detected on naïve CD4 T cells in the TCRβ transgenic animals ranged from less than 5000 to a maximum of about 30,000.
source: Species accumulation curves show that the total number of TCRα sequences we could detect on naïve CD4 T cells in the TCRβ transgenic animals ranged from less than 5000 to a maximum of about 30,000.
evidence: This is based on species accumulation curve analysis of sequencing data.

claim: The numbers of TCRα sequences found in CD4 naïve T cells from B6 mice are greater than 10^5 in number.
source: These numbers are less than those found in CD4 naïve T cells from B6 mice, which we found to be similar in number to those found on mouse CD8 T cells (Genolet et al., 2012), >than 105 in number (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on species accumulation curve analysis and comparison with published data.

claim: More than four times more TCRα sequences were apparent in mice expressing IAb versus IAs when paired with DOβWT.
source: The numbers of TCRα sequences that could partner with DOβWT in selection of CD4 T cells varied considerably with the selecting MHCII allele. More than four times more TCRα sequences were apparent in mice expressing IAb versus IAs (Figure 3B–D), perhaps because the TCR from which DOβWT is derived can be selected by IAb (Liu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on species accumulation curve data shown in Figure 3, with a speculative explanation.

claim: The effect of MHC allele on the numbers of selected TCRα chains was not evident in animals expressing DOβ48A.
source: This effect of MHC allele on the numbers of selected TCRα chains was not evident in animals expressing DOβ48A.
evidence: This is based on comparison of species accumulation curves for DOβ48A mice with different MHC alleles.

claim: The numbers of different TCRα chains associated with DOβ48A was lower than those associated with DOβWT regardless of the MHCII allele involved.
source: Notably, the numbers of different TCRα chains associated with DOβ48A was lower than those associated with DOβWT regardless of the MHCII allele involved, possibly because of the extra demands imposed on TCRα chains by the inadequate TCRβ chain lacking an important MHC contact residue, Y48 (Scott-Browne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on species accumulation curve data with a speculative explanation.

claim: The same combination of TRAV/TRAJ/CDR3 sequences were likely to appear in samples from mice of the same TCRβ and MHC genotype but were very unlikely to be shared with the T cells from mice expressing a different MHC allele.
source: Jaccard analyses showed that the same combination of TRAV/TRAJ/CDR3 sequences were likely to appear in samples from mice of the same TCRβ and MHC genotype but were very unlikely to be shared with the T cells from mice expressing a different MHC allele (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on Jaccard similarity analysis of TCRα sequences shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sequences that appear frequently in one mouse of a given genotype are more likely to be found in other mice of the same type.
source: Moreover, the fact that the values of the Anne Chao Jaccard analyses for mice of the same MHCII allele are much larger than those of the Jaccard analyses shows that sequences that appear frequently in one mouse of a given genotype are more likely to be found in other mice of the same type.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing Jaccard and Anne Chao Jaccard indices.

claim: Some sequences were repeated many times in all mice of a given MHCII type, whereas other sequences were rare.
source: Such a result is a manifestation of the fact that some sequences were repeated many times in all mice of a given MHCII type, whereas other sequences were rare.
evidence: This is an inference from the Anne Chao Jaccard analysis results.

claim: The uneven distribution of TCR sequences was not necessarily caused by expansion of single clones of T cells.
source: The phenomenon was not necessarily caused by expansion of single clones of T cells since, even in sets in which the CDR3α amino acid sequences were identical, the DNA sequences were not necessarily all the same (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DNA sequences underlying identical CDR3α amino acid sequences.

claim: The selected TCRα chains depended on the partner TCRβ, even when the selecting MHC allele was identical.
source: Similar analyses were applied to samples from mice in which the selecting MHCII allele was identical, but the partner TCRβ differed. The data show that the selected TCRα chains depended on the partner TCRβ, even when the selecting MHC allele was identical.
evidence: This is based on Jaccard similarity analyses comparing mice with the same MHC but different TCRβ.

claim: There was slightly more overlap if the co-selected TCRβs were different but the selecting MHCII alleles were identical than if the reverse were true.
source: Close inspection revealed, however, that there was slightly more overlap if the co-selected TCRβs were different but the selecting MHCII alleles were identical than if the reverse were true, that is the co-selected TCRβs were the same but the selecting MHCII alleles were different (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Fink and Bevan, 1978).
evidence: This is based on comparison of Jaccard indices shown in Figure 4C, D and supplement.

claim: TRAV usage on preselection thymocytes was similar, regardless of the MHC allele in the donor animal or the coexpressed TCRβ(s).
source: We first tested whether the expressed MHC haplotype might unexpectedly affect the nature of TRAVs expressed on preselection thymocytes. As shown in Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2, TRAV usage on preselection thymocytes was similar, regardless of the MHC allele in the donor animal or the coexpressed TCRβ(s).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAV usage in preselection thymocytes shown in Figure 5A and supplements.

claim: TRAVs whose genes are most proximal to the TRAJ locus (TRAVs 17–21) were frequently rearranged in preselection thymocytes.
source: TRAVs whose genes are most proximal to the TRAJ locus (TRAVs 17–21) were frequently rearranged, as predicted by previous studies (Villey et al., 1996; Shih et al., 2011; Genolet et al., 2012)
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAV usage in preselection thymocytes, consistent with previous studies.

claim: In preselection thymocytes, frequent rearrangements involving TRAV 1 and members of the TRAV 3, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 14 families were observed.
source: However, in preselection thymocytes we also observed frequent rearrangements involving TRAV 1 and members of the TRAV 3, 6, 7, 10, 11 and 14 families.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAV usage in preselection thymocytes.

claim: The selecting MHC allele affected the frequency with which different TRAVs were expressed on mature naïve CD4 T cells.
source: However, the selecting MHC allele affected the frequency with which different TRAVs were expressed on mature naïve CD4 T cells (Figure 5—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAV usage in mature CD4 T cells shown in Figure 5 supplements.

claim: Members of the TRAV5 family were used to some extent by CD4 T cells selected on IAb, but not by cells selected on IAf or IAs.
source: For example members of the TRAV5 family were used to some extent by CD4 T cells selected on IAb, but not by cells selected on IAf or IAs (compare Figure 5B,C with Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is based on comparison of TRAV usage data shown in Figure 5.

claim: CD4 T cells in DOβWT H2s mice were alone in their use of TRAV17.
source: On the other hand, CD4 T cells in DOβWT H2s mice were alone in their use of TRAV17 (Figure 5B,D and F).
evidence: This is based on TRAV usage data shown in Figure 5.

claim: TRAJ use by preselection thymocytes was similar regardless of the selecting MHC haplotype or co-expressed TCRβ.
source: TRAJ use by preselection thymocytes was similar regardless of the selecting MHC haplotype or co-expressed TCRβ (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAJ usage in preselection thymocytes shown in Figure 6A and supplements.

claim: TRAJ use by naïve CD4 T cells from B6 mice was fairly uniform across the locus.
source: TRAJ use by naïve CD4 T cells from B6 mice was fairly uniform across the locus (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAJ usage shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TRAJ use by T cells from mice expressing a single TCRβ was much more uneven and tended towards TRAJs whose genes were distal to the TRAV locus.
source: Unexpectedly, however, and in contrast to preselection thymocytes and naïve CD4 T cells from B6 mice, TRAJ use by T cells from mice expressing a single TCRβ was much more uneven and tended towards TRAJs whose genes were distal to the TRAV locus (Figure 6B–L).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAJ usage shown in Figure 6B-L.

claim: CD4 T cells in DOβWT animals used TRAJ21 most frequently regardless of MHC allele.
source: Regardless of MHC allele, CD4 T cells in DOβWT animals used TRAJ21 most frequently (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAJ usage shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: In DOβ48A mice, TRAJ 9, TRAJ 12 and TRAJs 9,15 and 31 dominated in H2b, H2f and H2s mice respectively.
source: The bias towards use of distal TRAJ genes was even more marked in animals expressing DOβ48A. In these mice TRAJ 9, TRAJ 12 and TRAJs 9,15 and 31 dominated in H2b, H2f and H2s mice respectively (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TRAJ usage shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: CD4 T cells selected on IAb had significantly shorter CDR3α lengths and fewer N region bases than their counterparts selected on IAf or IAs.
source: We compared the average lengths of CDR3αs and the predicted number of N region bases between mice expressing the same TCRβ and different MHCII alleles. CD4 T cells selected on IAb had significantly shorter CDR3α lengths and fewer N region bases than their counterparts selected on IAf or IAs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CDR3α lengths shown in Figure 7 supplement 1.

claim: The expressed CDR3α sequences in mice with a particular MHCII allele were very unlikely to be found in CD4 T cells of mice expressing a different MHCII allele, even if the co-selected TCRβ were the same.
source: The results were similar to those obtained when comparing the entire TCRα sequences. The expressed CDR3α sequences in mice with a particular MHCII allele were very unlikely to be found in CD4 T cells of mice expressing a different MHCII allele, even if the co-selected TCRβ were the same in the mice (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is based on Jaccard analysis of CDR3α sequences shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: CDR3α sequences co-selected with a particular TCRβ were unlikely to be shared with those co-selected with a different TCRβ, even if the selecting MHCII allele were the same.
source: Likewise, CDR3α sequences co-selected with a particular TCRβ were unlikely to be shared with those co-selected with a different TCRβ, even if the selecting MHCII allele were the same.
evidence: This is based on Jaccard analysis of CDR3α sequences.

claim: T cells expressing DOβWT and the same TRAV and TRAJ combinations, but selected on different MHCII alleles or with different TCRβs clearly had CDR3α sequences that were almost completely unique to the selecting MHCII alleles.
source: T cells expressing DOβWT and the same TRAV and TRAJ combinations, but selected on different MHCII alleles or with different TCRβs clearly had CDR3α sequences that were almost completely unique to the selecting MHCII alleles.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CDR3α sequences from the same TRAV/TRAJ pairs shown in Figure 8.

claim: Thymocytes with aromatic/hydrophobic amino acids at the tips of their CDR3β segments are biased towards MHC reactivity, regardless of the selecting MHCII allele.
source: A recent study has reported that thymocytes with aromatic/hydrophobic amino acids at the tips of their CDR3β segments are biased towards MHC reactivity, regardless of the selecting MHCII allele (Stadinski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The results show MHCII allele and TCRβ specific selection for particular amino acids at CDR3α positions.
source: The results show MHCII allele and TCRβ specific selection for particular amino acids and also changes in amino acid preference at CDR3α positions depending on the length of the CDR3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of amino acid usage at CDR3α positions shown in Figure 8 supplement 2.

claim: Positive selection involves interactions between TCRs and allele-specific amino acids of MHC in the thymus.
source: The simplest explanation for the effects of positive selection on the reactivity of mature T cells is that the phenomenon involves interactions between TCRs and allele-specific amino acids of MHC in the thymus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Positive selection may depend on interactions between TCRs and the MHC-bound self peptides.
source: However, since different MHC alleles will bind different self peptides, positive selection may instead or, in addition, depend on interactions between TCRs and the MHC-bound self peptides.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The allele of MHCII involved in positive selection affects the frequencies with which TRAV and TRAJ elements are selected.
source: The findings presented previously (Merkenschlager et al., 1994) and here, demonstrate that the allele of MHCII involved in positive selection affects the frequencies with which TRAV and TRAJ elements are selected and, most dramatically, the CDR3α sequences that appear on mature T cells, as previously indicated for CD8 T cells (Ferreira et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, supported by citations.

claim: The allele of MHCII involved in positive selection most dramatically affects the CDR3α sequences that appear on mature T cells.
source: The findings presented previously (Merkenschlager et al., 1994) and here, demonstrate that the allele of MHCII involved in positive selection affects the frequencies with which TRAV and TRAJ elements are selected and, most dramatically, the CDR3α sequences that appear on mature T cells, as previously indicated for CD8 T cells (Ferreira et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All three of the TCRα CDRs can play a role in positive selection.
source: We think it likely that all three of the TCRα CDRs can play a role in positive selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: CDR3α is involved in positive selection since the sequences in the center of this element vary depending on the selecting MHCII allele, even if the accompanying TRAV and TRAJ are the same.
source: However, clearly CDR3α is involved since the sequences in the center of this element vary depend on the selecting MHCII allele, even if the accompanying TRAV and TRAJ are the same (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Positive selection allele specificity involves recognition of both MHC and peptide.
source: Overall, the results strongly suggest that positive selection allele specificity involves recognition of both MHC and peptide (reviewed in (Klein et al., 2014; Vrisekoop et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results, supported by citations to reviews.

claim: The sequence of the TCRβ chain affects the TCRα and CDR3α that can participate in positive selection almost as much as the selecting MHC allele does.
source: The data here also show that the sequence of the TCRβ chain affects the TCRα and CDR3α that can participate in positive selection almost as much as the selecting MHC allele does.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data comparing different TCRβ chains.

claim: The TCRβ affects which TCRαs and which CDR3αs will be successful in positive selection.
source: Not only does the TCRβ affect which TCRαs and which CDR3αs will be successful, it also determines how many different TCRαs can do the job since, regardless of the MHCII allele involved, fewer TCRαs can be selected with DOβ48A than with DOβWT.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Fewer TCRαs can be selected with DOβ48A than with DOβWT regardless of the MHCII allele involved.
source: Not only does the TCRβ affect which TCRαs and which CDR3αs will be successful, it also determines how many different TCRαs can do the job since, regardless of the MHCII allele involved, fewer TCRαs can be selected with DOβ48A than with DOβWT.
evidence: This is based on species accumulation curve data.

claim: DOβ lacking an important MHC contact amino acid, the 'Y' at position 48, places more stringent requirements on TCRα for successful thymus selection.
source: These results are similar to those observed earlier that showed that fewer CD4 T cells are selected in DOβ48A-expressing versus DOβWT-expressing mice. Together these suggest that DOβ lacking an important MHC contact amino acid, the 'Y' at position 48, places more stringent requirements on TCRα for successful thymus selection (Scott-Browne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: The entire TCR sequence plays a role in positive selection.
source: Overall, the results show that the entire TCR sequence plays a role in positive selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data showing effects of TRAV, TRAJ, CDR3α, and TCRβ on selection.

claim: Competition for selection in the thymus has been previously demonstrated.
source: Probably it is caused by competition for selection in the thymus, a phenomenon that has been previously demonstrated (Martins et al., 2014; Visan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: In the thymus of a mouse expressing a single TCRβ, all thymocytes expressing an even approximately suitable TCRα have the opportunity to be positively selected.
source: In the thymus of a mouse expressing a single TCRβ, the immature thymocytes bear the same large number of TCRαs, and now all those expressing an even approximately suitable TCRα have the opportunity to be positively selected.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the larger number of TCRα sequences found in single TCRβ mice compared to predictions from wild-type mice.

claim: Each TCRβ chain can be successfully selected with up to 25 different TCRαs in humans and mice.
source: Based on the estimated numbers of TCRβs and TCRαs that appear in the periphery of an individual, it has previously been estimated that each TCRβ chain can be successfully selected with up to 25 different TCRαs (Arstila et al., 1999; Casrouge et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: For a single TCRβ, the number of possible TCRα partners is at least 3 orders of magnitude larger than previously estimated.
source: Yet here, and in previous studies, it appears that, for a single TCRβ, the number of possible TCRα partners is at least 3 orders of magnitude larger.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the species accumulation curve data showing thousands of TCRα sequences per single TCRβ.
